extracted.intended_audience: patent searchers, patent attorneys, inventors, and IP professionals conducting prior-art searches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing patent prior‑art searches, including strategy (broad-to-narrow), keyword development, database selection, use of classification systems, and documentation of results. Aimed at producing comprehensive searches to inform IP strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad to Narrow Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The broad to narrow research strategy is the foundation of many successful patent searches: (1) Identify main concepts of an invention; (2) Select a primary concept that all search results must have; (3) Add secondary concepts to narrow results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start wide to capture diverse relevant art, then iteratively narrow by adding secondary concepts. Use the primary concept as a required filter so all results are on‑topic. This approach helps balance recall and precision in search results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Your Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear understanding of scope, key features, functionalities, and potential applications; identify relevant keywords and search terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before searching, explicitly document the invention's boundaries and important technical features and use that to drive term selection and concept decomposition. Consider multiple functional descriptions and use cases to avoid missing relevant prior art framed differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop Comprehensive Keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for all possible keyword combinations: spelling variations (UK vs US English), keywords in foreign languages, historical terms for different patent classifications, synonyms and related terms, different levels of abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build exhaustive term lists and combinations. Include alternate spellings, translations, older terminology, broader and narrower concept terms, and synonyms. Test and refine keyword sets iteratively based on initial results and discovered vocabulary in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize Multiple Databases (patent and non‑patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple patent databases (e.g., USPTO Patent Public Search, Google Patents, Espacenet, WIPO PatentScope, Lens.org, DEPATISnet) and non‑patent literature sources (peer‑reviewed publications, dissertations, conference presentations, trade publications, standards documents, web archives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine searching across several patent databases and non‑patent literature to maximize coverage. Different platforms index different jurisdictions, older records, or provide better search tools; non‑patent literature often contains disclosures not in patent databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Patent Classification Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ classification systems such as CPC (Cooperative Patent Classification), IPC (International Patent Classification), USPC (older U.S. classification), and Japan‑specific F‑terms / FI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search by relevant classification codes in addition to keywords to find art described with different vocabulary. Use CPC/IPC for international reach and USPC/F‑terms when researching jurisdiction- or era-specific records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and Document Results (search logging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a search log to record search parameters, databases searched, date searched, results reviewed, inventor/assignee names searched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain systematic documentation of queries, filters, and dates to ensure reproducibility and to support prosecution/IP‑strategy decisions. Logging helps avoid duplicated effort and demonstrates diligence; include which results were reviewed and why they were relevant or excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Rejected, Pending, and Abandoned Applications as Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejected, pending, and abandoned patent applications can also be considered prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit searches to granted patents; examine published and unpublished applications and prosecution histories where available, since they may disclose relevant technology or affect novelty/obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform Citation Analysis (forward and backward)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation analysis (forward and backward) is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow cited references (backward citations) and citing patents/papers (forward citations) from key documents to discover related or derivative disclosures that keyword searches may miss. Use citation chains to map the development of a technology area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct Inventor and Assignee Searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor and assignee searches identify related work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search by authors, inventors, and assignees/companies to find other filings or publications by the same parties; this can reveal related projects, family filings, or iterations of similar inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check Patent Family Members Across Jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Family members across jurisdictions provide additional context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate family filings (same application filed in multiple countries) to find earlier or more detailed disclosures, different claim scopes, or prosecution outcomes that inform novelty and patentability assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize Completeness to Avoid Costly Mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Incomplete searches can lead to costly mistakes in IP strategy, given the significant amount of money invested in pre‑market research and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for thoroughness—incomplete or shallow searches risk missed prior art that can undermine filing, prosecution, or enforcement. Allocate sufficient time and resources, and combine strategies (keywords, classifications, citations, inventor/assignee lookups) to maximize coverage.
